90c3aa269c.q: How should internal communicators approach using AI for writing and content creation?
90c3aa269c.a: Amanda recommends not using AI to start from scratch for writing, as that tends to produce poor results. Instead, she uses AI to scale her writing by…
90c3aa269c.e: S01 EP2 - Balancing AI and human judgement in IC, with Amanda Atkinson
f: Don't start from scratch with AI—it produces poor results. Instead, begin with your own core narrative and use AI to adapt and scale it into supporting pieces like event invitations, Slack posts, and promotional copy. The real value emerges when you start with human work and use AI to enhance it, not the other way around.
Why starting with AI leads to a mess

Using AI as your first step in the writing process tends to generate generic, uninspired output that requires heavy reworking. Where you start with AI, you find yourself just getting a mess. The problem isn't that AI lacks capability—it's that without human direction rooted in your organisation's voice, values, and context, AI produces content that feels disconnected and requires substantial revision. This approach wastes time rather than saves it.
The winning approach: human foundation, AI acceleration

The most effective workflow begins with you writing the core message yourself. This might be a key memo, a strategic narrative, or your authentic take on a topic. Then use AI to enhance and challenge that work , multiplying it across different formats and channels. As discussed at length in this episode of Unprompted: Real AI in IC , internal communicators report that this sequence—human insight first, AI adaptation second—unlocks genuine productivity gains.

The practical application is immediate: write your all-hands talking points, then ask AI to turn that into a Slack announcement, an event invitation, or a calendar reminder in your preferred tone. AI becomes a scaling engine for work already grounded in human judgment and organisational knowledge. You maintain control, authenticity, and context while eliminating repetitive rewriting.

Amanda Atkinson combined post-event feedback data with original event objectives, then asked AI to identify gaps between emotional response and message absorption—revealing that while cultural connection was strong, key messaging around strategy and ways of working had not been fully absorbed.
Turning Event Data into Strategic Insight

When the Science Based Targets Initiative held its first all-staff off-site in years in Amsterdam, Amanda saw an opportunity to test a real strategic application of AI. Feedback was overwhelmingly positive—employees felt energized and connected. But "positive" doesn't always mean "strategically effective." She took the raw feedback data and combined it with the original session objectives and desired outcomes for each part of the event.

The next step was direct: Amanda fed both the feedback and the objectives to AI and asked it to identify gaps between what people felt emotionally and whether the strategic messages had truly been absorbed. This isn't AI replacing judgment—it's AI enhancing the analysis that Amanda herself would have to manually piece together , but faster and more systematically.
What the Data Revealed

The results told a clear story: cultural connection was strong , but key messaging around strategy and ways of working had not fully landed with the audience. That gap would have been harder to articulate without the structured AI analysis. Amanda now had a data-backed narrative for stakeholders—not just "people loved it," but "people felt connected, and here's where we need to reinforce strategy messaging next time."

Pair this with an AI-powered chief-of-staff agent that monitors your email, Slack, and Teams channels to flag urgent and overdue items, letting you focus your mental energy on high-impact decisions rather than triage.
Using AI as a collaborative thought partner

The shift from tool to partner starts with how you configure your AI. Instead of using ChatGPT or ChatGPT Enterprise only for one-off tasks, create distinct personas that represent different expertise domains. As Adele McIntosh explains in the Unprompted episode , she sets up personas like an internal comms expert, a marketing expert, and an engineering expert, then runs them through collaborative brainstorms on real strategic questions.

This approach surfaces cross-functional perspectives without requiring lengthy meetings . You get rapid iteration on messaging, audience strategy, or organizational challenges by prompting each persona with the same prompt and comparing their distinct angles. It's simultaneous thinking from multiple disciplines, compressed into minutes.
Automating awareness without losing human judgment

Beyond brainstorming, McIntosh created a chief-of-staff agent that monitors her communications in real-time across email, Slack, and Teams . This agent flags urgent items, reminds her of overdue follow-ups, and surfaces context she might have missed in the constant flow of messages and requests.

856a734074.q: How can internal communicators practically capture and synthesize organizational insights using AI?
856a734074.a: Amanda uses a personal Slack channel where she captures ideas, voice notes, videos, forwarded emails, and files throughout her day. She then synthesizes…
856a734074.e: S01 EP3 - Using AI as a strategic partner, with Erik Sebok
f: Build a personal Slack channel to capture raw insights throughout your day —ideas, voice notes, videos, forwarded emails, and files—then synthesize this collection regularly using AI tools like Gemini to extract principles and actionable checklists. This method removes friction from knowledge capture and transforms scattered feedback into structured communication frameworks without requiring additional meeting time.
A single channel as your thinking partner

Amanda Atkinson's approach starts simple: designate a dedicated Slack channel as your personal inbox for organizational signals . Throughout the day, she captures everything—quick observations from one-to-one meetings with leadership, tone shifts in team feedback, ideas that emerge during conversations, even forwarded emails that contain valuable context. No filtering, no editing at capture time. The goal is velocity, not polish.

This is not a journal or a brainstorm document. It's raw material deliberately gathered for later synthesis . Think of it as collecting fragments of organizational truth as they happen, before the context fades or the nuance gets lost in translation.
From capture to framework in one synthesis pass

Once or twice per week, Amanda reviews this accumulated material and feeds it into an AI synthesizer—in her case, Gemini. The AI doesn't generate her thinking; it helps her organize and extract the patterns she's already sensed. This synthesis step turns scattered observations into communication principles and practical checklists that directly inform her regular biweekly communications to the organization.

"You have to put time aside and put time in to learn and experiment and read and do the training and experiment again and that does take time there's no kind of shortcut to it really."

This approach combines AMAs with leadership, transparent viewpoints on ethical and environmental concerns, and continuous FAQs that evolve as organizational understanding develops.

The foundation is rejecting the "big launch" mentality. Instead of announcing AI adoption as a single organizational event, the strategy involves multiple touchpoints designed to address skepticism directly. As Adele McIntosh explains in the podcast , this means preparing leaders at every level—not just the C-suite—to have authentic conversations about both opportunity and concern.
Building trust through acknowledgment, not reassurance

The most effective framing doesn't dismiss fears about job displacement; it acknowledges them explicitly and positions AI as a tool that amplifies human capability rather than replaces it. At Arm, this involves crafting messaging that centers on human judgment and decision-making as irreplaceable, even as the technology changes what work looks like.

This requires preparation for managers. They become the primary communicators to their teams, so they need clear talking points, FAQs for difficult questions, and permission to say "I don't know yet." According to the approach detailed in this episode , organizations should provide managers with templates and frameworks so their answers feel consistent without being robotic.
Making the narrative evolve deliberately

04cfa63c35.q: What is the biggest challenge of rolling out generative AI to employees compared to other technology implementations?
04cfa63c35.a: Unlike rolling out a tool such as Salesforce — where success is clearly defined and adoption is eventually guaranteed — generative AI is totally unbounded:…
04cfa63c35.e: S01 EP4 - Getting people on board with AI at work, with Charlotte Halligan
f: The core challenge is that generative AI is entirely unbounded: unlike rolling out a tool such as Salesforce — where success is clearly defined and adoption is eventually guaranteed — neither society nor organizations have yet defined what success or the future state actually looks like. Without a concrete destination to communicate, internal teams have no future-state story to rally employees around, and every individual arrives at the rollout with a wildly different starting point shaped by external narratives the organization simply cannot control.

With a conventional technology deployment, communicators can say with confidence: here is what the world looks like once we've crossed the finish line. That narrative anchor is what drives engagement and manages anxiety. Generative AI removes it entirely. Employees bring their own pre-formed assumptions — from news coverage, social media, and public debate — into the workplace on day one, and those assumptions vary enormously. Some arrive convinced AI will take their jobs; others dismiss it as hype; others are already power users of tools like ChatGPT in their personal lives. The organization inherits all of that variation without having shaped any of it.

The absence of a locked-down future-state vision also has direct knock-on effects on messaging. As Charlotte Halligan experienced first-hand when leading an enterprise-level generative AI rollout across a complex global organization, key messaging frameworks can take months to stabilize — in her case, roughly six months into the rollout before core messaging was fully locked down. This is not a communications failure; it reflects a genuine organizational reality that has no equivalent in a standard technology programme. The full episode on Listenly explores how she navigated these compounding challenges across multiple roles, legislations, and geographies.
"It's not necessarily that AI is going to take your job, but somebody who knows AI is going to take your job. So you kind of have to get on the bus or get off the bus."
— Charlotte Halligan, Comms Leader / Internal Communications Leader

61bae3abcd.q: How can internal communicators identify which problems are suitable for AI agent solutions?
61bae3abcd.a: Rebecca identifies needs through data and evidence, such as from internal comms surveys. For example, the annual leave assistant was created after survey results showed people struggled with returning from time off. She also relies on her intuitive listening skills as an internal communicator to spot friction points and grumbles in the organization where AI could help individuals have better conversations.
61bae3abcd.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: Combine hard evidence from employee surveys with intuitive listening to spot where AI agents can genuinely help. Rebecca Lindsay at Hyper Exponential uses internal communications survey data to identify friction points—like her annual leave assistant, created after survey results revealed employees struggled when returning from time off—and pairs this with her instinct for catching workplace grumbles where better conversations could transform the employee experience.
Data-Driven Discovery Meets Employee Listening

The foundation of identifying suitable AI agent problems starts with real survey results and feedback loops . When Rebecca Lindsay saw that return-to-work transitions were causing stress among her team at Hyper Exponential, she didn't guess—she let the data guide the solution. An annual leave assistant was built directly in response to this evidence, solving a concrete pain point rather than chasing AI adoption for its own sake.

However, data alone isn't enough. As an internal communicator, Rebecca relies on her lived experience of organizational life—the conversations in corridors, the repeated complaints, the moments when people express frustration about processes that feel unnecessarily complicated. This intuitive listening amplifies what surveys reveal , surfacing problems that employees might not articulate in formal feedback channels. The combination of quantitative evidence and qualitative observation creates a map of where AI agents can make a real difference.

Discussed in depth in Unprompted: Real AI in IC , Rebecca's approach reflects a broader principle: prioritize employee outcomes over technology trends . The Institute of Internal Comms index 2026 highlights that people are time poor at the moment, making this need for friction-reduction even more acute. An AI agent should ease the burden, not create another step in an already taxed workflow.
"We want to be giving you the tools to do great comms yourself, and that is precisely what AI can enable us to do at scale."

ff9429022b.q: What are the key steps for implementing and rolling out an AI agent in an organization?
ff9429022b.a: The three steps are: first, identifying the need through data or observed friction; second, creating the agent itself; third, behaviorally designing the rollout so it reaches the right people at the right time. Rebecca integrated the annual leave assistant with the HR platform so employees received the agent link when they submitted annual leave, ensuring adoption at the moment of need.
ff9429022b.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: AI agent rollout requires three sequential steps: identify the need through data or observed friction , create the agent itself, then design the behavioral rollout so it reaches users at their moment of greatest need. Success depends on placing the agent at the exact point where employees encounter the problem it solves.
Starting with Evidence, Not Assumptions

The first step is not to guess which problems your organization should solve. Data from surveys or direct feedback reveals the actual pain points that employees face daily. This grounds your AI investment in real friction, not intuition.

As Rebecca Lindsay explains in the episode , Hyper Exponential identified the annual leave assistant as a priority after survey data showed this was genuinely pulling people's attention away from other work.
Timing Is Everything: The Moment-of-Need Principle

Once the agent exists, the rollout strategy determines whether employees actually use it . Launching an agent and hoping people find it is passive; designing the moment of adoption is active adoption strategy.

34c02dce79.q: What prompt engineering techniques help ensure better AI agent outcomes?
34c02dce79.a: Rebecca recommends asking the AI tool to clarify your requirements before running the prompt, saying 'you don't know what you don't know.' She also suggests adding instructions to the AI that it should ask clarifying questions, which it can remember for future interactions. She emphasizes being really clear about what knowledge the agent should draw on and what you want to achieve.
34c02dce79.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: Start by asking the AI tool to clarify your requirements before running the full prompt —Rebecca Lindsay emphasizes you don't know what you don't know. Instruct the AI to ask follow-up questions and remember them for future interactions, and be explicit about which knowledge sources the agent should draw from and what outcome you're trying to achieve.
Three foundational principles for stronger prompts

The first step is pre-clarification. Rather than launching straight into a complex request, ask the AI to help you define what you actually need. This upfront conversation prevents misalignment later and forces both you and the agent to name assumptions that might otherwise remain hidden. As Rebecca explains in the episode , many people rush into their request without first unpacking what they actually want to achieve.

Second, embed permission for the agent to ask clarifying questions within your initial prompt. This transforms the interaction from one-directional to conversational. By instructing the AI to probe deeper, you allow it to surface gaps in your brief and propose refinements. Rebecca describes this as giving the agent a voice to shape the outcome, not just execute a predetermined instruction.

Third, be explicit about scope and knowledge boundaries. Define which sources, tools, or data the agent should reference and which it should avoid. Clarity on what the agent is supposed to know—and what it should ignore—prevents hallucinations and ensures outputs stay grounded in your organizational context. This is particularly important at Hyper Exponential, where the tone of voice agent and annual leave assistant had to be trained to draw only from specific internal documentation and policies.
"We want to be giving you the tools to do great comms yourself, and that is precisely what AI can enable us to do at scale."

9133122d83.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: Rebecca Lindsay built an agent that scores written communications against emotional intelligence principles using a defined rubric, but it only analyzes text and has no access to human context—missing critical nuance that matters to real conversations.
A rubric-driven approach to emotional tone

The agent works by evaluating written communications—emails, messages, announcements—against key emotional intelligence principles . Rebecca built it to give instant feedback on tone and approach, mimicking what an emotionally aware reviewer would flag.
The system uses a clear scoring rubric to evaluate each message. This keeps the feedback consistent and reproducible, though it also locks the agent into a fixed framework.
The blind spot: context and nuance

The agent's biggest limitation is that it cannot see the human context . An emotionally intelligent response depends heavily on who wrote the message, why, for whom, and what happened before—none of which the agent can access.

e8d4559e05.q: What is the role of layered data in building more effective internal communications strategies with AI?
e8d4559e05.a: Rebecca compiles a personal internal comms brain containing multiple data sources: internal comms survey results, employee satisfaction data, event feedback, and external research like the Institute of Internal Comms indexes. She stresses that individual data points are good, but layering multiple points of data together creates immensely more powerful insights and richer context for all comms elements.
e8d4559e05.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: Individual data points are useful, but combining multiple sources—internal surveys, employee satisfaction data, event feedback, and external research indexes—creates exponentially richer insights for AI-powered communications decisions. This layered approach gives your AI agents and human team the full context they need to craft more effective, targeted messaging.

The power of layered data lies in depth. Rather than relying on a single metric or feedback channel, Rebecca Lindsay compiles a personal internal comms brain that pulls from multiple simultaneous data streams . This includes hard metrics like internal comms survey results and employee satisfaction scores, alongside qualitative inputs like event feedback and benchmarked research from reputable sources.

As detailed in this episode of Unprompted: Real AI in IC , external research frameworks like the Institute of Internal Comms index become particularly valuable when layered with your own organizational data. These indexes reveal macro trends—such as the finding that people are increasingly time poor —which you can then cross-reference with your own employee feedback to understand how that pressure manifests in your specific culture.
Why a single data point falls short

One survey result, one satisfaction score, or one event feedback comment tells you what happened, but not why it matters or how to act on it. Layering changes that calculus entirely. When survey data aligns with event feedback and external benchmarks all point to the same tension, your AI agents have unambiguous direction on where to focus comms efforts.

Rebecca emphasizes that richer context enables richer output from both AI tools and human judgment. Instead of defaulting to generic messaging, you can craft internal communications that directly address the specific pressures and priorities your people face. As discussed in the full podcast episode , this principle applies whether you're designing an AI agent or writing a strategic brief for your leadership team.

AI agents and brains can help individuals write their own messages with guidance, supporting managers and teams to have better conversations. 12267c1bcd.e: S01 EP1 - Experimenting with AI agents in internal comms, with Rebecca Lindsay (hyperexponential)
f: AI is shifting internal communicators from being 'post boxes' that distribute messages to enablers who give others the tools to communicate well themselves . Rather than creating all content centrally, communicators can now guide managers and teams through AI-powered agents that help them craft their own messages, turning the role into one of strategic support at scale.

The transformation addresses a real challenge facing internal comms teams today. As explained in Unprompted: Real AI in IC , people across organizations are time-poor, yet they still need to communicate effectively with their teams. Instead of bottlenecking all requests through a central comms function, AI agents can distribute the capability to communicate well directly to the people who need it most—managers, team leads, and individual contributors.

This shift means internal communicators stop being the gatekeepers of every message. Instead, they become architects of systems that empower others. As Rebecca Lindsay describes it: "We want to be giving you the tools to do great comms yourself, and that is precisely what AI can enable us to do at scale."
From bottleneck to enabler: redefining the internal comms role

Traditional internal communications operates as a centralized function—messages flow through the comms team, creating inevitable delays and a dependency on their capacity. This model breaks down when organizations need rapid, localized communication from managers and team leads. AI agents solve this by placing communication tools directly in the hands of those who need them , guided by frameworks and guardrails set by the internal comms team.

The role becomes less about authoring every message and more about ensuring that those messages—written by dozens or hundreds of people across the organization—align with brand voice, tone, and strategic intent. Rebecca Lindsay's work at Hyper Exponential demonstrates this in practice through AI agents that support everything from annual leave messaging to emotionally intelligent communications checking, freeing internal comms to focus on strategy rather than production.
